payload.title: Switching Off the Sky
paragraphs: For most of human history the night sky was one of the few sights everyone shared. A child in a mountain village and an astronomer in a capital city looked up at the same few thousand stars. Today more than a third of the world's population cannot see the Milky Way from home, and not because the stars have dimmed. The ground beneath them has begun to glow.

The usual response is to blame the sheer number of lamps, yet the real culprit is design. A great deal of outdoor lighting points sideways or upward, spilling far beyond the path or car park it was bought to illuminate. Cheap white LEDs have made matters worse in an unexpected way: because they are so efficient, councils simply install more of them, and their blue-rich glare scatters through the atmosphere far more readily than the warm sodium light it replaced.

What makes light pollution unusual among environmental problems is that it disappears the moment it is addressed. A shielded lamp aimed at the pavement and dimmed after midnight costs less to run and restores the sky above it that same night. Moths return to the hedgerows within a season. No decades-long cleanup is needed, no new technology waits to be invented; what is missing is only the decision to point the light downwards.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Light pollution is caused mainly by badly aimed lighting rather than by the number of lamps, and unlike most environmental damage it can be undone almost immediately.
Because modern LEDs use very little electricity, cities should install as many of them as possible and accept that the stars will no longer be visible.
Astronomers have exaggerated the loss of the night sky, since the stars themselves are gradually growing fainter for natural reasons.
The only realistic way to see the Milky Way again is for people to move out of cities and into mountain villages.

questions.after: of the switch: because running costs fell, towns simply put up more lights than before.

payload.title: The Toaster on the Table
paragraphs: On the first Saturday of each month, the hall behind the town library fills with broken things. People arrive carrying lamps that flicker, kettles that leak and coats with torn linings, and they queue for a seat beside one of the volunteers. The event is called a repair cafe, and nobody is charged; the only rule is that the owner must sit at the table and watch the repair being done.

That rule is the point of the whole exercise. A volunteer could work far faster alone, but then the visitor would leave with a working toaster and nothing else. Sitting beside the tools, people discover that a dead appliance often has one loose wire, and that opening a case is a matter of patience rather than expertise. Roughly six items in ten leave the hall working again.

The organisers are careful not to claim too much. A monthly session cannot compete with the volume of goods a single shop sells in a morning, and some products are sealed so tightly that no volunteer can open them without breaking them. Still, the visitors who return tend to arrive with better questions, and a few now bring their neighbours' appliances as well as their own.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: A repair cafe fixes household objects for free, but its real value is that owners sit beside the volunteers and learn that many repairs are within their own reach.
Repair cafes have already replaced ordinary shops in many towns because volunteers can work faster than professional technicians.
The main purpose of a repair cafe is to raise money for the town library through the small fees charged for each repair.
Most household appliances are now impossible to open, so repair cafes have quietly abandoned their original aim.

questions.after: the quantity of new goods sold in local shops, but they still see the habit it teaches as worthwhile.

questions.sentence: What they take home, then, is a small piece of confidence as well as a working object.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
